title: Signal No. 3 by Thursday
note: Fictional unit. Your continuity plan and the Medical Director’s decisions come first.
intro: You manage a twelve-station unit in Tacloban City. On Tuesday morning, PAGASA forecasts a typhoon making landfall on Thursday night, with Signal No. 3 expected for your area. Your Thursday and Friday patients are due during the storm and just after it.

choices.text: Meet the Medical Director today to decide on early dialysis; then notify patients of revised schedules, top up fuel and water, and move records and equipment above flood level.
choices.feedback: The advisory phase is when decisions are made. The Medical Director decides on early sessions; your job is to make that decision happen.
choices.then: The Medical Director moves all Thursday and Friday patients to Wednesday and early Thursday morning.

choices.text: Wait for Thursday’s bulletin; the track may change.
choices.feedback: Waiting for landfall to decide on early dialysis is one of the common failure modes. By Thursday there is no time to reschedule 24 patients.
choices.then: You call the Medical Director that afternoon. Thursday and Friday patients are moved to Wednesday and early Thursday.

choices.text: Reschedule the Thursday and Friday patients yourself and tell the Medical Director afterward.
choices.feedback: Acting early is right, but early dialysis is a treatment change: the Medical Director decides. Bring the plan, not a fait accompli.
choices.then: The Medical Director confirms the plan with one change for two patients.

n2.scene: You expect grid power to fail. The generator burns about 25 liters an hour at full load, and you have 600 liters. Twelve machines at a dialysate flow of 500 mL a minute, plus about 90 liters an hour of other use, draw on 2,700 liters of usable treated-water storage.
n2.prompt: Which runs out first on generator power?

choices.text: Water: 12 × 0.5 × 60 = 360 + 90 = 450 L an hour, so about 6 hours. Fuel lasts about 24 hours. Arrange the water tanker under contract.
choices.feedback: Operating autonomy is the smaller of the two. Water is the binding constraint: one full shift, not two. More diesel would not help.

choices.text: Fuel: order another 600 liters of diesel.
choices.feedback: Run the numbers: fuel lasts about 24 hours, water about 6. Solving the wrong shortage wastes the hours you have.
choices.then: You recalculate and call the water tanker under the standing contract.

choices.text: Both seem fine for a day; check again if the power goes.
choices.feedback: Water lasts about 6 hours at full load, not a day. Find the binding constraint before the outage, not during it.
choices.then: You run the numbers and call the water tanker.

n3.prompt: What must every patient leave with before the unit closes?

choices.text: A printed emergency information sheet (prescription, access type, serology, PhilHealth Dialysis Database status, contacts, partner units) and the dietitian’s emergency diet, plus a confirmed place to shelter; and you print the patient contact list.
choices.feedback: If the unit cannot open, another unit needs these details to treat them. And a patient list that lives only in the electronic system is lost when the power or network goes.

vitals.patients: All treated early; sheets given; list printed

choices.text: A reminder to come back on Saturday; the records are all in the system.
choices.feedback: “The list in the dead computer” is a classic failure. Print the contacts, and give each patient what another unit would need.
choices.then: You print the sheets and the contact list before closing.

vitals.patients: All treated early; sheets given; list printed

choices.text: A copy of their prescription only.
choices.feedback: A start, but a partner unit also needs the access type, serology, and PhilHealth Dialysis Database status, and the patient needs the emergency diet.
choices.then: You complete the sheets and print the contact list.

vitals.patients: All treated early; sheets given; list printed

n4.scene: The typhoon has passed. Grid power returned at 05:00. The building is dry. Staff are arriving and patients are calling to ask when they can come.

choices.text: Inspect building, power, and water; have the water tested and released before any treatment; reopen in phases, highest-risk patients first; and contact every patient.
choices.feedback: Interrupted power affects the water system as well as the machines. The water is tested and released before treatment, and the Medical Director’s priority list sets who comes first.

choices.text: Open all twelve stations as soon as staff arrive; the power is back.
choices.feedback: Power back does not mean the water is safe. Treating on untested water after an outage risks every patient on the floor.
choices.then: The water technician stops the start and tests the water. It is released at 09:00 and the unit reopens in phases.

choices.text: Reopen in order of the usual schedule.
choices.feedback: After a closure, the patients with the longest gap and highest risk come first, on the Medical Director’s list. And the water still has to be released before anyone starts.
choices.then: The water is released at 09:00, and the Medical Director’s priority list sets the order.

n5.scene: By noon, nurses have reached 33 of 36 patients. Three cannot be reached; one lives in a barangay where the bridge is out.

choices.text: Ask the barangay health workers and local officials to find the three; for the patient who cannot cross, arrange transfer to a partner unit with the emergency sheet, on the Medical Director’s decision.
choices.feedback: Your job is to know where every patient is and to make the clinical decision happen. Partner units and the emergency sheet exist for exactly this.

choices.text: Wait for them to call; they know the unit is open.
choices.feedback: A patient who cannot be reached may not have a phone, power, or a way across. Waiting can cost a life.
Calling continues, but bring in the barangay health workers and the partner-unit plan now, not after another day.

end.title: Accounted for
end.text: The barangay health workers find two patients in an evacuation center; the third is taken across by a rescue boat and treated at the partner unit with her emergency sheet. You add to the plan: test the reverse osmosis output on generator power at the next load test, and send one transient patient through the partner unit agreement each year.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Decide early. The Medical Director decides on early dialysis in the advisory phase; you make it happen.
  • Find the binding constraint: water usually runs out before fuel.
  • Paper beats the dead computer: emergency sheets for patients, a printed contact list for you.
  • Reopen safely: water tested and released, highest-risk patients first.
  • Account for every patient, with barangay health workers and partner units.

See Outage autonomy, A phased typhoon plan and Common failure modes.
